The following family makes the extensive-source issue concrete without invoking interacting dynamics or an unknown stationary state.

Set

 $\gamma=1,\qquad H=0,\qquad
\rho_0=(I/2)^{\otimes n},
\qquad
\mathcal D_i=\frac12(\mathcal R_{0,i}-\mathrm{Id}),$ with fixed rational  $\eta>0$ . At the rational time  $T=1$ , computational measurement gives independent signs with bias

 $b=\frac{\eta}{2+\eta}
\left(1-e^{-(1+\eta/2)}\right)>0:
\qquad
P_b(x)=2^{-n}\prod_{i=1}^n(1+bx_i).
\tag{8}$ This is inside the native class for any declared positive Hamiltonian bound. Its law has an elementary polynomial-bit sampler: compute the scalar bias to  $O(\epsilon/n)$ , round the coin probabilities to  $O(\log(n/\epsilon))$  bits, and use a fixed number of random bits per site.

Direct absolute signed sampling is exponentially expensive

Write

 $P_b=\bigotimes_i(u_i+\nu_i),
\qquad
u_i(x_i)=\frac12,\quad
\nu_i(x_i)=\frac b2x_i.$ Every correction has zero mass and  $\|\nu_i\|_1=b$ . Nevertheless, the absolute mass of the subset expansion is

 $Z_{\rm abs}
=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}b^{|S|}
=(1+b)^n.
\tag{9}$ A direct sign-corrected expansion has exponentially small average sign. Resumming the independent factors removes that cost completely. Thus the sign cost is a property of this representation.

Sublinear total-order truncation loses the typical output region

Consider the exactly normalized signed truncation

 $q_L(x)=2^{-n}
\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq[n]\\|S|\le L}}b^{|S|}x_S,
\qquad x_S=\prod_{i\in S}x_i.
\tag{10}$ Define the event

 $A_n=\left\{x:\sum_i x_i\ge \frac{bn}{2}\right\}.$ Hoeffding’s inequality gives

 $P_b(A_n)\ge1-e^{-b^2n/8},
\qquad
U(A_n)\le e^{-b^2n/8},$ where  $U$  is uniform.

Walsh orthogonality and Cauchy–Schwarz give

 $|q_L|(A_n)
\le
e^{-b^2n/16}
\left(\sum_{j=0}^L\binom nj b^{2j}\right)^{1/2}.
\tag{11}$ For  $L\le n/2$ ,

 $\sum_{j=0}^L\binom nj b^{2j}
\le e^{n h(L/n)},$ with  $h$  the binary entropy using natural logarithms. Therefore, for every  $L=o(n)$ ,

 $|q_L|(A_n)\longrightarrow0,
\qquad
\frac12\|P_b-q_L\|_1\ge1-o(1).
\tag{12}$ The second expression is a half- $L^1$  error against a signed measure; it is not being called TV between probability laws.
